claims.text: Melt-spinning produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbon.
The melt-spinning cooling rate is approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
A brief isothermal anneal at approximately 780 K for a few minutes should be applied immediately after melt-spinning.
Approximately 780 K is near 0.8 times the alloy's lowest reheating crystallization temperature.
The proposed 780 K anneal remains below the relevant early-stage crystallization boundary.
Sub-crystallization annealing enhances structural relaxation and reduces internal stresses and free-volume defects.
Reducing internal stresses and free-volume defects lowers the density of crystalline nucleation sites.
At 780 K, atomic rearrangement can produce structural relaxation without crossing the critical temperature for nucleation.
Structural relaxation minimizes the driving force for primary crystallization during subsequent heating.
The anneal will shift crystallization temperatures upward and thereby improve thermal stability.
Relative to the as-quenched ribbon, the annealed alloy will retain a greater amorphous fraction and form fewer primary crystalline phases during reheating.
The untreated rapidly quenched alloy crystallizes eutectic and non-eutectic primary phases near 960–1206 K during reheating.
Cooling rate strongly affects the phase composition and microstructure of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Slower cooling produces a complex multiphase crystalline microstructure, whereas very rapid melt-spinning produces an amorphous structure.
The slower cooling condition relevant to the comparison is approximately 52 K/s.
The intervention should be effective only for melt-spun material and annealing temperatures below approximately 800 K.
The intervention may be ineffective after slower cooling because extensive crystallization has already occurred.
Phosphorus addition enhances the glass-forming ability of this alloy during rapid cooling.
